//: Composite indexes AURIX's queries need.
Deploy with:  firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes
Firestore creates single-field indexes automatically, so most queries here
need nothing — including both search paths. Each filters on a single array
field (`searchTokens`, with `array-contains`) and applies no second filter
and no ordering, so the automatic array index serves them. They are listed
under fieldOverrides below to make the array indexing explicit and to
document the query each exists for, not because the default would be wrong.
The shared playlist catalogue's discovery query — the one that makes an
import by one user findable by every other — is that array-contains on
`/playlists`. It has no uid filter and no second clause, which is why it
needs no composite index at all.
Two queries genuinely need composite indexes, and both are equality-only
pairs, which Firestore will not serve from single-field indexes:
1. The de-duplication fallback in
FirestoreGlobalPlaylistService.findBySource, which filters `source`
and `sourceId` together. The normal path is a direct document read on
the derived id (see PlaylistKey) and touches no index; this covers a
document written under a different id scheme.
2. The same pair on a user's own playlists, for
FirestorePlaylistService.findOwnBySource — the migration path.
Both are served by one entry: a COLLECTION-scoped index on a collection
group applies to every collection with that name, and both `/playlists` and
`/users/{uid}/playlists` are named `playlists`.
Deliberately absent: an index on likedTracks(createdAt), on
playlists(updatedAt), on playlistTracks(position), or on
playlists(importedByUserId). The first three are single-field orderings and
are automatic. The fourth is a single-field equality filter — the Library
screen's `watchImportedBy` — and it is deliberately not paired with an
orderBy: sorting one user's own imports client-side costs nothing and saves
a composite index, so the automatic single-field index serves it.
The song catalogue search index.
`searchTokens` holds up to 180 prefix strings per song, and the
array-contains query in FirestoreCatalogService.search is what makes a
keystroke an indexed lookup instead of a collection scan.
ARRAY_CONFIG is what supports array-contains. ASCENDING/DESCENDING
ordering on this field is switched off deliberately: nothing orders by
it, and each one would be another 180 index entries written per song.
The playlist search index — the one every user's search reads.
Covers `/playlists` (the shared catalogue, queried by
FirestoreGlobalPlaylistService.search) and `/users/{uid}/playlists`,
since a COLLECTION-scoped override applies to every collection with
this name.
Playlist documents carry a much smaller token array than songs — one
title rather than a title, artist and album — so the write cost of
publishing a playlist is a fraction of the cost of publishing its
songs. That is what makes prefix search over the whole catalogue cheap
enough to do on every keystroke.
